sources.entry: Patterns in confusing explanations, Julia Evans

summary.title: Patterns in confusing explanations
summary.one_liner: You learn 13 common patterns that make technical explanations hard to follow (such as outdated audience assumptions, strained analogies, and missing "why") and practical fixes for each.
keywords: explaining wrong way without saying wrong
takeaways: Test explanations with people who don't already know the topic, since experts share the same blind spots.
Write for one specific reader, such as a friend or a past version of yourself, to keep the knowledge level consistent.
Keep analogies to a single idea, and prefer realistic code examples over contrived ones.
Open with a concrete experience and explain the 'why' behind a technology, not just a feature list.
Say up front when something is a mistake, and back up claims with examples the reader can run.
summary.summary: Julia Evans reflects on why many technical explanations confuse her and lists 13 recurring patterns, from outdated assumptions about the reader's knowledge to 'what' without 'why'. Each pattern is illustrated with examples from real documentation such as the Git book, Python lambda and Java interface examples, and Kubernetes' homepage. For every pattern she offers an alternative approach, such as testing explanations with newcomers, using realistic examples, and giving personal reasons for choosing a technology. The post is written as a self-critical guide for the author's own writing as well as for readers.
